title: Ἵππος καὶ δάκρυα
titleEn: The Horse and the Tears — Odyssey 8.487–586
about: Odysseus praises the minstrel Demodocus and asks him for a new song, the making of the wooden horse and the sack of Troy. Demodocus sings it, and the hero who is hearing his own exploits wets his cheeks with tears, as a captured woman weeps over her fallen husband. Only Alcinous notices. He stops the song and turns to his guest with the questions a host owes: his name, his country and his city, so that the Phaeacian ships can take him home, and why he weeps for the fate of Troy.

sentences.t: Δημόδοκ’, ἔξοχα δή σε βροτῶν αἰνίζομ’ ἁπάντων.
sentences.l: “Demodocus, outstandingly indeed you, of mortals, I praise, of all.
sentences.i: “Demodocus, I praise you above all mortal men.
sentences.n: Δημόδοκ’ is the vocative with its last vowel elided. αἰνίζομαι means 'praise, commend'; ἔξοχα is an adverb, 'outstandingly', and βροτῶν ἁπάντων is a genitive of comparison, 'above all mortals'; δή adds emphasis and σε is the object. This is Odysseus, whose introduction ended the last part; his speech runs to 8.498, so the opening quotation mark stands here, on its first words.

sentences.t: ἢ σέ γε μοῦσ’ ἐδίδαξε, Διὸς πάϊς, ἢ σέ γ’ Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l: either you, indeed, the Muse taught, the child of Zeus, or you, indeed, Apollo;
sentences.i: Either the Muse taught you, the child of Zeus, or Apollo did;
sentences.n: ἢ … ἢ is 'either … or', and γε puts stress on each σέ: it was you, one god or the other. μοῦσ’ is μοῦσα with the final vowel elided. Διὸς πάϊς is 'child of Zeus', πάϊς being the Homeric shape of παῖς. ἐδίδαξε, from διδάσκω 'teach', keeps its augment here, though Homer's past tenses often drop it.

sentences.t:
λίην γὰρ κατὰ κόσμον Ἀχαιῶν οἶτον ἀείδεις,
ὅσσ’ ἔρξαν τ’ ἔπαθόν τε καὶ ὅσσ’ ἐμόγησαν Ἀχαιοί,
ὥς τέ που ἢ αὐτὸς παρεὼν ἢ ἄλλου ἀκούσας.
sentences.i: for you sing the fate of the Achaeans in very good order, all that they did and suffered and all that they toiled through, as though you had been there yourself or had heard it from another.
sentences.n: κατὰ κόσμον is 'in due order, in proper sequence'; κόσμος returns in the next unit with a different sense. οἶτον is the accusative of οἶτος 'fate, lot', usually a sad one, and it comes back at 578. ὅσσ’ … ὅσσ’ 'all that … and all that' opens two clauses whose verbs are three aorists, all with the augment: ἔρξαν (ῥέζω 'do'), ἔπαθον (πάσχω 'suffer') and ἐμόγησαν (μογέω 'toil'). Ἀχαιῶν and Ἀχαιοί are the same name for the Greek army, and both are translated. ὥς τέ που is 'as if perhaps'; παρεών is the participle of πάρειμι 'be present', and ἄλλου ἀκούσας 'having heard from another' has a genitive of the person heard from.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ μετάβηθι καὶ ἵππου κόσμον ἄεισον
δουρατέου, τὸν Ἐπειὸς ἐποίησεν σὺν Ἀθήνῃ,
ὅν ποτ’ ἐς ἀκρόπολιν δόλον ἤγαγε δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἀνδρῶν ἐμπλήσας οἵ ῥ’ Ἴλιον ἐξαλάπαξαν.
sentences.l:
But come now, change-over, and of the horse the ordering sing,
the wooden one, which Epeius made with Athena,
which once to the citadel as a trick led heavenly Odysseus,
having filled it with men, who Ilios sacked.
sentences.i: But come now, change your theme and sing of the contriving of the wooden horse, which Epeius made with Athena's help, and which heavenly Odysseus once led up into the citadel as a trick, after filling it with the men who sacked Ilios.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is 'but come now'. μετάβηθι is the aorist imperative of μεταβαίνω 'change over', that is, pass to another subject. ἵππου κόσμον is 'the ordering of the horse', κόσμος here meaning how it was contrived and fitted out, not 'proper order' as in 489. δουρατέου is 'wooden' (Attic δούρειος). ἐποίησεν 'made' is augmented; Ἐπειός is the builder and σὺν Ἀθήνῃ 'with Athena' names his helper. ὅν is a relative pronoun ('which'), and δόλον stands in apposition to it, 'as a trick'. ἐμπλήσας, aorist participle of ἐμπίμπλημι 'fill', governs ἀνδρῶν in the genitive; οἵ ῥ’ is οἳ ῥα. ἐξαλάπαξαν is the aorist of ἐξαλαπάζω 'sack utterly'. δῖος 'heavenly' is the stock epithet of Odysseus and is always so rendered.

sentences.t:
αἴ κεν δή μοι ταῦτα κατὰ μοῖραν καταλέξῃς,
αὐτίκ’ ἐγὼ πᾶσιν μυθήσομαι ἀνθρώποισιν,
ὡς ἄρα τοι πρόφρων θεὸς ὤπασε θέσπιν ἀοιδήν.
sentences.i: If you recount this to me as is fitting, then at once I will tell all men that a god with a ready mind has granted you inspired song.”
sentences.n: αἴ κεν is epic for εἰ ἄν, and with the aorist subjunctive καταλέξῃς 'you recount' it makes a future condition; κατὰ μοῖραν is 'according to what is fitting'. αὐτίκ’ is 'at once' and μυθήσομαι the future 'I will tell'. ὡς ἄρα 'that, then' opens what he will say. πρόφρων is 'ready-minded, willing'; ὤπασε is the aorist of ὀπάζω 'grant'. θέσπιν is the accusative of θέσπις 'inspired, god-spoken', usually explained as θεός plus the root of ἔπος 'word', though the old compound is not certain. θεός has no article, so 'a god': Odysseus leaves open whether it was the Muse or Apollo of 488. The closing quotation mark ends his speech.

sentences.t: ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ ὁρμηθεὶς θεοῦ ἤρχετο, φαῖνε δ’ ἀοιδήν,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and he, stirred, began from the god, and made-appear his song,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the minstrel, stirred to it, began with the god and brought his song to light,
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ’ is 'So he spoke' (φάτο, the unaugmented form of ἔφατο, with its last vowel elided); ὁ is 'he', in Homer a pronoun, here the minstrel. ὁρμηθείς is the aorist passive participle of ὁρμάω 'set in motion, impel': he is stirred by Odysseus' request. θεοῦ ἤρχετο is 'began from the god', ἄρχομαι taking the genitive of the point of departure; the phrase does not say whether he invokes the god or is set going by him. φαῖνε, imperfect of φαίνω, is 'made appear, brought to light'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν ἑλὼν ὡς οἱ μὲν ἐυσσέλμων ἐπὶ νηῶν
βάντες ἀπέπλειον, πῦρ ἐν κλισίῃσι βαλόντες,
Ἀργεῖοι, τοὶ δ’ ἤδη ἀγακλυτὸν ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα
ἥατ’ ἐνὶ Τρώων ἀγορῇ κεκαλυμμένοι ἵππῳ·
sentences.l:
taking-up from there how they, on the well-benched ships
having embarked, sailed away, fire into the huts having cast,
the Argives, while the others already round renowned Odysseus
sat in the Trojans' assembly-place, hidden by the horse;
sentences.i: taking up the tale at the point where the Argives, going aboard their well-benched ships, sailed away with fire cast into the huts, while the rest, gathered round renowned Odysseus, were already sitting in the Trojan place of assembly, hidden by the horse;
sentences.n: ἔνθεν ἑλών is 'taking it from there', and ὡς 'how, where' opens the story he takes up. ἐυσσέλμων is 'well-benched'; βάντες is the aorist participle of βαίνω, and ἀπέπλειον the imperfect of ἀποπλέω. κλισίῃσι, dative plural of κλισίη, is 'huts', the shelters of the camp. Ἀργεῖοι 'Argives' is another name for the Greeks. οἱ μέν … τοὶ δέ is 'some … others', τοί being the pronoun 'they'. ἀγακλυτόν is 'renowned'. ἥατ’ is ἥατο, third plural imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit'; κεκαλυμμένοι is the perfect participle of καλύπτω, 'hidden'. ἀγορῇ is here the place of assembly, not the meeting itself.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ γάρ μιν Τρῶες ἐς ἀκρόπολιν ἐρύσαντο.
sentences.l: for the Trojans themselves to the citadel had dragged it.
sentences.i: for the Trojans themselves had dragged it up into the citadel.
sentences.n: γάρ explains how the horse came to stand in the Trojan place of assembly. αὐτοί, 'themselves', puts the blame on the Trojans. μιν is 'it', the horse, a Homeric pronoun with no article. ἐρύσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐρύω 'drag, haul'; the same verb, as ἐρύσαντας, appears at 508.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὁ μὲν ἑστήκει, τοὶ δ’ ἄκριτα πόλλ’ ἀγόρευον
ἥμενοι ἀμφ’ αὐτόν·
sentences.l:
So it stood, but they, many indiscriminate things, spoke
sitting around it;
sentences.i: So the horse stood there, while the Trojans, sitting round it, said many confused things;
sentences.n: ὁ μέν … τοὶ δέ is 'the one … the others': ὁ is the horse, τοί the Trojans. ἑστήκει is a pluperfect with the sense 'was standing'. ἀγόρευον is imperfect, 'were speaking'. ἄκριτα πόλλ’ is 'many things without discrimination', that is confused, undecided talk (ἄκριτος 'not sorted out'). ἥμενοι is the participle of ἧμαι 'sit'. The ano teleia falls inside line 506, so the next unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
τρίχα δέ σφισιν ἥνδανε βουλή,
ἠὲ διαπλῆξαι κοῖλον δόρυ νηλέι χαλκῷ,
ἢ κατὰ πετράων βαλέειν ἐρύσαντας ἐπ’ ἄκρης,
ἢ ἐάαν μέγ’ ἄγαλμα θεῶν θελκτήριον εἶναι,
sentences.l:
and in three ways to them was pleasing the counsel:
either to cleave through the hollow timber with pitiless bronze,
or down from the rocks to hurl it, having dragged it to a height,
or to let it be a great delight of the gods, a propitiation,
sentences.i: and their counsel was divided three ways: to split the hollow timber open with pitiless bronze, or to drag it to a height and hurl it down from the rocks, or to leave it as a great offering to soothe the gods,
sentences.n: τρίχα is 'in three parts, three ways'; σφισιν is 'to them' and ἥνδανε 'was pleasing' (ἁνδάνω). Three infinitives follow, one for each plan: διαπλῆξαι 'cleave through' (διαπλήσσω), βαλέειν 'hurl' (the uncontracted -έειν) with κατὰ πετράων 'down from the rocks', and ἐάαν 'to let be' (uncontracted ἐᾶν). ἐρύσαντας, 'having dragged it', is the same verb as in 504. δόρυ is 'timber', the horse's wooden body. νηλέι is 'pitiless', the standing epithet of bronze. ἄγαλμα is a thing that delights, a gift given in honour (later 'statue'), and θελκτήριον, from θέλγω 'charm, soothe', means 'a means of appeasing': the horse would be a placating offering to the gods. The unit ends at the comma of 509, because the sentence would otherwise run to five lines.

sentences.t: τῇ περ δὴ καὶ ἔπειτα τελευτήσεσθαι ἔμελλεν·
sentences.l: in which very way indeed also afterwards to be brought-to-pass it was destined;
sentences.i: and in that very way, indeed, it was afterwards to be brought to pass;
sentences.n: τῇ περ δὴ is 'in the very way in which', τῇ being the relative. τελευτήσεσθαι is the future middle infinitive of τελευτάω 'bring to an end', used as a passive, 'to be accomplished'. ἔμελλεν 'was destined, was about to' takes it. The narrator steps outside the scene: of the three plans the third is the one that would come about, as the next lines say.

sentences.t:
αἶσα γὰρ ἦν ἀπολέσθαι, ἐπὴν πόλις ἀμφικαλύψῃ
δουράτεον μέγαν ἵππον, ὅθ’ ἥατο πάντες ἄριστοι
Ἀργείων Τρώεσσι φόνον καὶ κῆρα φέροντες.
sentences.l:
for it was fated to perish, when the city should enfold
the wooden great horse, where sat all the best
of the Argives, bringing to the Trojans slaughter and doom.
sentences.i: For it was fated that the city should perish once it had enfolded the great wooden horse, where all the best of the Argives sat, bringing slaughter and doom to the Trojans.
sentences.n: αἶσα ἦν is 'it was their portion, it was fated'; ἀπολέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive 'to perish'. ἐπήν with the aorist subjunctive ἀμφικαλύψῃ is 'when once it has enfolded' (ἀμφικαλύπτω 'cover round'); the verb returns at 569, where the danger is turned against the Phaeacians. δουράτεον is 'wooden'. ὅθ’ is 'where', and ἥατο the imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit'. Line 513 is word for word the last line of 4.271–273.

sentences.t:
ἤειδεν δ’ ὡς ἄστυ διέπραθον υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
ἱππόθεν ἐκχύμενοι, κοῖλον λόχον ἐκπρολιπόντες.
sentences.l:
And he sang how the town they sacked, the sons of the Achaeans,
from the horse pouring out, the hollow ambush having left.
sentences.i: And he sang how the sons of the Achaeans sacked the town, pouring out from the horse and leaving the hollow ambush behind.
sentences.n: ἤειδεν is the augmented imperfect of ἀείδω 'sing'; the next line has the unaugmented ἄειδε. ὡς 'how' opens the story told. διέπραθον is the aorist of διαπέρθω 'sack utterly'. υἷες Ἀχαιῶν 'sons of the Achaeans' is a fixed periphrasis for the Greek warriors. ἱππόθεν is 'from the horse' (suffix -θεν). ἐκχύμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἐκχέω 'pour out': the men pour out of the horse like liquid. ἐκπρολιπόντες, from ἐκπρολείπω, carries two preverbs, 'leaving out and forth'. λόχον is 'ambush', the body of men lying in wait and the hollow place where they lay.

sentences.t:
ἄλλον δ’ ἄλλῃ ἄειδε πόλιν κεραϊζέμεν αἰπήν,
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσῆα προτὶ δώματα Δηιφόβοιο
βήμεναι, ἠύτ’ Ἄρηα σὺν ἀντιθέῳ Μενελάῳ.
sentences.l:
and one this way, another that, he sang, to ravage the steep city,
but Odysseus to the house of Deiphobus
to go, like Ares, with godlike Menelaus.
sentences.i: and he sang how they ravaged the steep city, one here and another there, and how Odysseus went to the house of Deiphobus, like Ares, with godlike Menelaus.
sentences.n: ἄλλον δ’ ἄλλῃ is 'one man one way, another another'. The infinitives κεραϊζέμεν 'to ravage' (the -έμεν ending) and βήμεναι 'to go' (aorist infinitive, Attic βῆναι) depend on ἄειδε: 'he sang that …'. αἰπήν 'steep, sheer' is said of a city on a height. προτί is πρός, and Δηιφόβοιο a genitive in -οιο; Deiphobus is a Trojan prince, a son of Priam. ἠύτ’ is 'like, as'. Ἄρηα is the accusative of Ἄρης, and ἀντιθέῳ 'godlike' is the stock epithet of Menelaus here.

sentences.t:
κεῖθι δὴ αἰνότατον πόλεμον φάτο τολμήσαντα
νικῆσαι καὶ ἔπειτα διὰ μεγάθυμον Ἀθήνην.
sentences.l:
There indeed most-dread war he said, having dared,
to have won, and afterwards through great-hearted Athena.
sentences.i: There, he said, Odysseus dared the most dread of wars, and in the end won it, through great-hearted Athena.
sentences.n: κεῖθι is 'there' (Attic ἐκεῖ). φάτο is 'he said', unaugmented, and takes an accusative and infinitive: 'that he, having dared …, won'. τολμήσαντα, aorist participle of τολμάω 'dare', agrees with the Odysseus of 517, who is not named again here. αἰνότατον, superlative of αἰνός 'dread', qualifies πόλεμον. καὶ ἔπειτα is 'and afterwards, in the end'. διά with the accusative means 'through, thanks to'; μεγάθυμον is 'great-hearted'.

sentences.t: ταῦτ’ ἄρ’ ἀοιδὸς ἄειδε περικλυτός·
sentences.l: These things then the minstrel was singing, far-famed;
sentences.i: These were the things the far-famed minstrel sang;
sentences.n: ταῦτ’ ἄρ’ is 'these things, then'. ἄειδε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀείδω 'sing'. ἀοιδός is 'minstrel', and περικλυτός 'far-famed' is his epithet. The ano teleia falls mid-line, and Odysseus' reaction opens the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
τήκετο, δάκρυ δ’ ἔδευεν ὑπὸ βλεφάροισι παρειάς.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
melted, and a tear wetted, from beneath the eyelids, his cheeks.
sentences.i: but Odysseus melted, and the tears wet his cheeks from beneath his eyelids.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ is 'but', turning from the singer to the listener. τήκετο is the imperfect middle of τήκω 'melt': he dissolved in weeping. ἔδευεν is the imperfect of δεύω 'wet'. δάκρυ is a collective singular, 'tears'. βλεφάροισι is a dative plural in -οισι, and ὑπό with the dative means 'beneath'; παρειάς is the accusative plural of παρειά 'cheek'.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ γυνὴ κλαίῃσι φίλον πόσιν ἀμφιπεσοῦσα,
ὅς τε ἑῆς πρόσθεν πόλιος λαῶν τε πέσῃσιν,
ἄστεϊ καὶ τεκέεσσιν ἀμύνων νηλεὲς ἦμαρ·
sentences.i: As a woman weeps when she has flung herself round her dear husband, who has fallen before his own city and his people, warding off the pitiless day from town and children;
sentences.n: ὡς δέ opens a simile, answered by ὣς Ὀδυσεύς at 531. κλαίῃσι is a subjunctive in -σι (Attic κλαίῃ), giving a general picture: 'as a woman weeps'. ἀμφιπεσοῦσα is the aorist participle of ἀμφιπίπτω 'fall about, throw oneself round'. ὅς τε has the epic τε, marking a general truth. ἑῆς is 'his own' (ἑός), πόλιος the genitive of πόλις, and πέσῃσιν the aorist subjunctive of πίπτω 'fall'. ἄστεϊ is the dative of ἄστυ, τεκέεσσιν the dative plural of τέκος. ἀμύνων 'warding off' takes the dative of those defended and the accusative of the danger: νηλεὲς ἦμαρ, 'the pitiless day', the day of doom. The warrior hero is compared to a woman.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν τὸν θνήσκοντα καὶ ἀσπαίροντα ἰδοῦσα
ἀμφ’ αὐτῷ χυμένη λίγα κωκύει·
sentences.l:
she, him dying and gasping having seen,
about him poured-out, shrilly wails;
sentences.i: she, seeing him dying and gasping, pours herself out around him and wails shrilly;
sentences.n: ἡ μέν is 'she', a pronoun. τὸν θνήσκοντα καὶ ἀσπαίροντα is 'him dying and gasping' (ἀσπαίρω 'gasp, struggle'); ἰδοῦσα is the aorist participle of ὁράω. χυμένη is the aorist middle participle of χέω 'pour', literally 'having poured herself' about him; ἐκχύμενοι at 515 is the same verb. λίγα is an adverb of λιγύς 'clear, shrill'. κωκύει 'wails' is present, the tense of the general picture.

sentences.t:
οἱ δέ τ’ ὄπισθε
κόπτοντες δούρεσσι μετάφρενον ἠδὲ καὶ ὤμους
εἴρερον εἰσανάγουσι, πόνον τ’ ἐχέμεν καὶ ὀιζύν·
sentences.i: while behind her they strike her back and shoulders with their spears and lead her up into slavery, to have toil and misery;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ τ’ is 'and they', the captors, left unnamed; ὄπισθε is 'behind'. κόπτοντες 'striking' takes δούρεσσι 'with spears' (dative plural in -εσσι of δόρυ) and the accusatives μετάφρενον 'the back' and ὤμους 'shoulders'. εἰσανάγουσι is 'lead up into'. εἴρερον is 'slavery'; its origin is obscure, but the sense is secure from the passage. ἐχέμεν is the infinitive ἔχειν in its -έμεν shape, expressing purpose: 'to have toil and misery'. ὀιζύν is the accusative of ὀιζύς 'misery'.

sentences.t: τῆς δ’ ἐλεεινοτάτῳ ἄχεϊ φθινύθουσι παρειαί·
sentences.l: and hers, with most-pitiable grief, waste away the cheeks;
sentences.i: and her cheeks waste away in the most pitiable grief;
sentences.n: τῆς is 'her', a pronoun. ἐλεεινοτάτῳ is the superlative of ἐλεεινός 'pitiable', from ἔλεος 'pity'; it returns as ἐλεεινόν at 531. ἄχεϊ is the dative of ἄχος 'grief'. φθινύθουσι is 'waste away' (φθινύθω, a longer form of φθίνω), and παρειαί, nominative plural, is its subject.

sentences.t: ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς ἐλεεινὸν ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι δάκρυον εἶβεν.
sentences.l: so Odysseus a pitiable tear from beneath his brows shed.
sentences.i: So Odysseus shed a pitiable tear from beneath his brows.
sentences.n: ὣς 'so' answers ὡς δέ of 523 and completes the simile. Ὀδυσεύς has a single σ here, Ὀδυσσεύς at 521, a difference of metre only. ἐλεεινόν 'pitiable' is the adjective of 530, here agreeing with δάκρυον. ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι is 'beneath the brows' (dative plural of ὀφρύς). δάκρυον is a longer form of δάκρυ 'tear'. εἶβεν is the imperfect of εἴβω 'let fall, shed', a poetic verb.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλους μὲν πάντας ἐλάνθανε δάκρυα λείβων,
Ἀλκίνοος δέ μιν οἶος ἐπεφράσατ’ ἠδ’ ἐνόησεν,
ἥμενος ἄγχ’ αὐτοῦ, βαρὺ δὲ στενάχοντος ἄκουσεν.
sentences.l:
Then all the others he escaped, tears pouring,
but Alcinous, him alone, noticed and perceived,
sitting near him, and heavily groaning he heard.
sentences.i: He escaped the notice of all the others as he poured out his tears, but Alcinous alone noticed him and understood, sitting close beside him, and heard him groaning heavily.
sentences.n: These three lines are 8.93–95 repeated word for word. ἐλάνθανε is the imperfect of λανθάνω 'escape notice of' and takes ἄλλους πάντας as its object, with the participle λείβων 'pouring' saying what he did unnoticed. μιν is 'him', and οἶος 'alone'. ἐπεφράσατ’ (φράζομαι 'notice') and ἐνόησεν are two aorists, 'noticed and perceived'. ἥμενος is 'sitting', ἄγχ’ αὐτοῦ 'near him'; ἄκουσεν 'heard' governs the genitive στενάχοντος 'him groaning'.

sentences.t: αἶψα δὲ Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.l: And at once among the oar-loving Phaeacians he spoke:
sentences.i: And at once he spoke among the oar-loving Phaeacians:
sentences.n: This line is 8.96 repeated. αἶψα is 'at once'. Φαιήκεσσι φιληρέτμοισι is a dative in -εσσι and -οισι; φιληρέτμοισι is 'oar-loving', from φίλος and ἐρετμόν 'oar'. μετηύδα is 'spoke among', a speech made to the whole company, and it stands before the colon that opens Alcinous' words.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτε, Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες,
Δημόδοκος δ’ ἤδη σχεθέτω φόρμιγγα λίγειαν·
sentences.l:
“Hear me, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians,
and Demodocus, now, let him hold-back the clear-sounding lyre;
sentences.i: “Hear me, leaders and lords of the Phaeacians, and let Demodocus now hold back his clear-sounding lyre;
sentences.n: κέκλυτε 'hear me' is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω, the call that opens an address to a company; line 536 is the same as 7.186. Φαιήκων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is 'leaders and lords of the Phaeacians', ἠδέ being 'and'. σχεθέτω is the third person aorist imperative of ἔχω, 'let him hold back', that is stop playing; φόρμιγγα λίγειαν is 'the clear-sounding lyre'. δ’ ἤδη is 'and now'. Alcinous' speech runs to the end of the part, and the opening quotation mark stands here.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πως πάντεσσι χαριζόμενος τάδ’ ἀείδει.
sentences.l: for not in any way to all pleasing these things he sings.
sentences.i: for in singing this he is not quite pleasing everyone.
sentences.n: οὐ … πως is 'not in any way', softened in English to 'not quite'. χαριζόμενος is 'gratifying, pleasing', with πάντεσσι in the dative (-εσσι). τάδ’ is 'these things', the object of ἀείδει 'sings'.

sentences.t:
ἐξ οὗ δορπέομέν τε καὶ ὤρορε θεῖος ἀοιδός,
ἐκ τοῦ δ’ οὔ πω παύσατ’ ὀιζυροῖο γόοιο
ὁ ξεῖνος·
sentences.i: Ever since we began to dine and the divine minstrel started up, the stranger has not once ceased from his woeful lamentation;
sentences.n: ἐξ οὗ and ἐκ τοῦ are 'from which time' and 'from that time'. δορπέομεν is 'we dine' (δορπέω). ὤρορε is a reduplicated aorist of ὄρνυμι 'rouse'; the sense here is that the minstrel stirred into song, the object being left to be understood, and the exact construction is not certain. θεῖος 'divine' is the epithet of the minstrel. παύσατο, aorist middle of παύω 'cease', takes the genitive ὀιζυροῖο γόοιο 'from woeful lamentation' (ὀιζυρός 'wretched, woeful'). ὁ ξεῖνος is 'the stranger', where ὁ is very nearly the later article.

sentences.t: μάλα πού μιν ἄχος φρένας ἀμφιβέβηκεν.
sentences.l: very much, I suppose, him grief his mind has come-around.
sentences.i: no doubt grief has closed about his mind.
sentences.n: πού is 'I suppose, no doubt'. μιν … φρένας is 'him … in his mind', the whole and the part in the accusative. ἄχος is 'grief'. ἀμφιβέβηκεν is the perfect of ἀμφιβαίνω 'stand around, enfold', with present sense: grief has come round his mind and stays there.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ ὁ μὲν σχεθέτω, ἵν’ ὁμῶς τερπώμεθα πάντες,
ξεινοδόκοι καὶ ξεῖνος, ἐπεὶ πολὺ κάλλιον οὕτως·
sentences.l:
But come, let him hold-back, so that alike we may delight, all,
hosts and guest, since much finer so;
sentences.i: But come, let him hold back, so that we may all take pleasure alike, hosts and guest, since it is much better so;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγ’ is 'but come'. ὁ μέν is 'he', Demodocus, set against 'all' in the next words; σχεθέτω is as at 537. ἵν’ 'so that' takes the subjunctive τερπώμεθα, from τέρπω, in the middle 'take pleasure'. ὁμῶς is 'alike'. ξεινοδόκοι are 'hosts', those who receive a guest, and ξεῖνος 'guest'. πολὺ κάλλιον is 'much finer, much better'.

sentences.t:
εἵνεκα γὰρ ξείνοιο τάδ’ αἰδοίοιο τέτυκται,
πομπὴ καὶ φίλα δῶρα, τά οἱ δίδομεν φιλέοντες.
sentences.l:
for on account of the stranger, the revered one, these things have been made ready,
escort and dear gifts, which to him we give, loving him.
sentences.i: for it is for the sake of the revered stranger that these things have been made ready, the escort and the dear gifts that we give him out of friendship;
sentences.n: εἵνεκα is ἕνεκα 'for the sake of', governing the genitive ξείνοιο αἰδοίοιο (-οιο for -ου), 'the revered stranger'; αἰδοῖος is 'worthy of reverence', from αἰδώς. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω, 'have been made ready'. πομπὴ καὶ φίλα δῶρα, 'escort and dear gifts', says what τάδ’ means. τά οἱ is 'which … to him'. φιλέοντες is 'loving', in the uncontracted form of φιλέω.

sentences.t:
ἀντὶ κασιγνήτου ξεῖνός θ’ ἱκέτης τε τέτυκται
ἀνέρι, ὅς τ’ ὀλίγον περ ἐπιψαύῃ πραπίδεσσι.
sentences.l:
In place of a brother, a stranger and a suppliant has been made
to a man, who even a little touches with his wits.
sentences.i: For a man who has even a little sense, a stranger and a suppliant stands in place of a brother.
sentences.n: ἀντὶ κασιγνήτου is 'in place of a brother' (κασίγνητος 'brother'). τέτυκται is 'is (made)', as in 544. ἀνέρι is ἀνδρί, dative of ἀνήρ. ὅς τ’ … ἐπιψαύῃ is a general relative clause with the epic τε and the subjunctive; ἐπιψαύω 'touch, lay hold of' has πραπίδεσσι 'wits, understanding' in the instrumental dative: 'who touches with his wits even a little', that is, has even a little sense.

sentences.t:
τῷ νῦν μηδὲ σὺ κεῦθε νοήμασι κερδαλέοισιν
ὅττι κέ σ’ εἴρωμαι·
sentences.l:
Therefore now do not you either conceal, with cunning thoughts,
whatever I shall ask you;
sentences.i: So now do not you either hide, with cunning thoughts, whatever I ask you;
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore', a dative of ὁ meaning 'on that account'. μηδὲ σύ is 'nor you'. κεῦθε is the imperative of κεύθω 'hide, conceal'. νοήμασι κερδαλέοισιν is 'with cunning thoughts': κερδαλέος is 'cunning, gain-seeking', from κέρδος. ὅττι is ὅ τι 'whatever', and εἴρωμαι the present subjunctive of εἴρομαι 'ask', with κε.

sentences.t: φάσθαι δέ σε κάλλιόν ἐστιν.
sentences.l: and to speak, for you, is finer.
sentences.i: and it is better for you to speak.
sentences.n: φάσθαι is the epic infinitive of φημί, 'to speak'. σε is the accusative subject of the infinitive, 'that you speak'. κάλλιον is the comparative of καλός, 'finer, better', the same word as at 543.

sentences.t:
εἴπ’ ὄνομ’ ὅττι σε κεῖθι κάλεον μήτηρ τε πατήρ τε
ἄλλοι θ’ οἳ κατὰ ἄστυ καὶ οἳ περιναιετάουσιν.
sentences.l:
Tell the name by which they there used-to-call you, mother and father
and the others, both those in the town and those who dwell around.
sentences.i: Tell me the name by which your mother and father used to call you there, and the others too, those in the town and those living round about.
sentences.n: εἴπ’ is εἰπέ, the aorist imperative of λέγω 'say', with its final vowel elided. ὄνομ’ is 'name', and ὅττι is ὅ τι 'what', a second accusative after κάλεον: 'the name, what they called you'. κεῖθι is 'there', in his own country. κάλεον is 'used to call': imperfect of καλέω, uncontracted and unaugmented (Attic ἐκάλουν). ἄλλοι θ’ οἳ … οἳ is 'and the others, both those who … and those who …'. κατὰ ἄστυ is 'through the town', and περιναιετάουσιν 'dwell around' (uncontracted -άουσιν, Attic -ῶσιν).

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γάρ τις πάμπαν ἀνώνυμός ἐστ’ ἀνθρώπων,
οὐ κακὸς οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλός, ἐπὴν τὰ πρῶτα γένηται,
ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πᾶσι τίθενται, ἐπεί κε τέκωσι, τοκῆες.
sentences.l:
For not indeed is any wholly nameless of men,
not bad, nor indeed good, when first he has come-to-be,
but on all they place one, once they have begotten, the parents.
sentences.i: For no one among men is wholly without a name, neither bad nor good, once he has first come into being; parents give one to every child as soon as they have begotten it.
sentences.n: ἀνώνυμος is 'nameless' (ἀ- and ὄνομα); ἐστ’ is ἐστί, and ἀνθρώπων is a partitive genitive, 'of men'. οὐ κακὸς οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλός is 'neither bad nor good', in apposition to τις. ἐπὴν τὰ πρῶτα γένηται is 'as soon as he has come into being', with τὰ πρῶτα 'at first'. ἐπὶ … τίθενται is ἐπιτίθεμαι 'put upon, give', in tmesis, with its object (a name) left unsaid. ἐπεί κε τέκωσι is 'once they have begotten', τέκωσι being the aorist subjunctive of τίκτω; τοκῆες is 'parents'.

sentences.t: εἰπὲ δέ μοι γαῖάν τε·
sentences.l: And tell me the country too;
sentences.i: And tell me of your country too:
sentences.n: εἰπὲ δέ μοι is 'and tell me'. γαῖάν τε is 'the country also'; τε looks ahead to the pair that follows. γαῖα is the country as a whole, so the word is rendered 'country' where it stands in a list beside δῆμος 'land' and πόλις 'city'. The ano teleia falls mid-line, and the next unit fills out the request.

sentences.t:
τεὴν δῆμόν τε πόλιν τε,
ὄφρα σε τῇ πέμπωσι τιτυσκόμεναι φρεσὶ νῆες·
sentences.l:
your land and city,
so that thither may convey you, aiming with their minds, the ships;
sentences.i: your land and your city, so that the ships, aiming with their minds, may carry you there;
sentences.n: τεήν is 'your own' (τεός = σός); it is feminine, so it agrees with πόλιν (and γαῖαν), and its sense 'your' covers the whole list; δῆμον is the land of a community, and πόλιν 'city'. ὄφρα is 'so that', with the subjunctive πέμπωσι 'convey'; νῆες 'ships' is its subject, and τῇ is 'thither'. τιτυσκόμεναι is the participle of τιτύσκομαι 'aim at, direct one's course', with φρεσί 'with their minds', which prepares for what he says of the Phaeacian ships in the next lines.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Φαιήκεσσι κυβερνητῆρες ἔασιν,
οὐδέ τι πηδάλι’ ἔστι, τά τ’ ἄλλαι νῆες ἔχουσιν·
sentences.l:
for not to Phaeacians steersmen are,
nor any steering-oars are, which other ships have;
sentences.i: for the Phaeacians have no steersmen, and there are no steering-oars of the kind that other ships have;
sentences.n: Φαιήκεσσι is a dative of possession, 'to the Phaeacians there are': ἔασιν is εἰσί. κυβερνητῆρες are 'steersmen'. πηδάλι’ is πηδάλια, the steering-oars at the stern by which an ancient ship was steered. τά τ’ … ἔχουσιν is 'which … have', with the epic τε; ἄλλαι is 'other'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αὐταὶ ἴσασι νοήματα καὶ φρένας ἀνδρῶν,
καὶ πάντων ἴσασι πόλιας καὶ πίονας ἀγροὺς
ἀνθρώπων, καὶ λαῖτμα τάχισθ’ ἁλὸς ἐκπερόωσιν
ἠέρι καὶ νεφέλῃ κεκαλυμμέναι·
sentences.l:
but themselves they know the thoughts and the minds of men,
and of all they know the cities and the rich fields
of men, and the gulf of the salt-sea most swiftly they cross,
hidden in mist and cloud;
sentences.i: but the ships themselves know the thoughts and minds of men, and they know the cities and rich fields of all people, and they cross the gulf of the salt sea most swiftly, hidden in mist and cloud;
sentences.n: αὐταί is 'themselves', feminine plural for the ships. ἴσασι is the third plural of οἶδα, 'they know', and νοήματα καὶ φρένας is 'thoughts and minds'. λαῖτμα is 'gulf, the depths of the sea'; ἁλός is the genitive of ἅλς 'salt-sea'. τάχισθ’ is τάχιστα 'most swiftly', elided. ἐκπερόωσιν is 'cross over' (ἐκπεράω, uncontracted -όωσιν). ἠέρι καὶ νεφέλῃ is 'in mist and cloud', datives; κεκαλυμμέναι is the perfect participle of καλύπτω 'hide', as κεκαλυμμένοι at 503.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ ποτέ σφιν
οὔτε τι πημανθῆναι ἔπι δέος οὔτ’ ἀπολέσθαι.
sentences.l:
and never for them
is there fear either of being harmed at all or of perishing.
sentences.i: and they never have any fear of being harmed or of perishing.
sentences.n: σφιν is 'to them', the ships. ἔπι with the accent on its first syllable stands for ἔπεστι 'there is upon': the preposition does the work of the verb. δέος is 'fear'. οὔτε τι … οὔτε is 'neither at all … nor'. πημανθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of πημαίνω 'harm', from πῆμα 'woe'; ἀπολέσθαι is 'to perish', as at 511.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τόδ’ ὥς ποτε πατρὸς ἐγὼν εἰπόντος ἄκουσα
Ναυσιθόου, ὃς ἔφασκε Ποσειδάων’ ἀγάσασθαι
ἡμῖν, οὕνεκα πομποὶ ἀπήμονές εἰμεν ἁπάντων.
sentences.l:
But this, as once, from my father saying it I heard,
Nausithous, who used-to-say that Poseidon was resentful
of us, because escorts harmless we are of all.
sentences.i: But this I once heard my father Nausithous say: he used to say that Poseidon resented us because we are harmless escorts of all men.
sentences.n: ὥς is 'how, as', introducing what he heard. ἀκούω takes the genitive of the speaker: πατρὸς εἰπόντος is 'my father saying'. ἐγὼν is ἐγώ with a movable -ν, and Ναυσιθόου is the genitive of Nausithous. ἔφασκε is 'used to say', an iterative in -σκ-. Ποσειδάων’ is the accusative Ποσειδάωνα, elided, and ἀγάσασθαι, the aorist middle infinitive of ἀγάομαι, means 'be resentful of', with the dative ἡμῖν. οὕνεκα is 'because', and εἰμεν is ἐσμέν. πομποὶ ἀπήμονες is 'harmless escorts', ἀπήμων being ἀ- and πῆμα.

sentences.t:
φῆ ποτὲ Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν ἐυεργέα νῆα
ἐκ πομπῆς ἀνιοῦσαν ἐν ἠεροειδέι πόντῳ
ῥαισέμεναι, μέγα δ’ ἧμιν ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψειν.
sentences.l:
He said that some day of the Phaeacian men a well-made ship
coming back from an escort on the misty-looking sea
he would smash, and a great mountain over our city would enfold.
sentences.i: He said that some day he would smash a well-made ship of the Phaeacians as she came back from an escort on the misty-looking sea, and would enfold our city in a great mountain.
sentences.n: φῆ is 'he said' (ἔφη). It governs accusative and infinitive: ῥαισέμεναι 'would smash' (ῥαίω) and ἀμφικαλύψειν 'would enfold', both future infinitives, whose subject is Poseidon, still understood from 565. ποτέ here looks forward, 'some day'. ἐυεργέα is 'well-made'. ἐκ πομπῆς ἀνιοῦσαν is 'coming back from an escort' (ἄνειμι). ἠεροειδέι is 'misty-looking'. ἧμιν is ἡμῖν, and ἀμφικαλύψειν is the verb of 511, where the Trojans' city enfolds the horse.

sentences.t: ὣς ἀγόρευ’ ὁ γέρων·
sentences.l: So the old man spoke;
sentences.i: So the old man spoke;
sentences.n: ὣς ἀγόρευ’ is 'so he spoke' (ἀγόρευε elided), the line that closes a speech, here closing Nausithous' words as Alcinous reports them. ὁ γέρων is 'the old man'.

sentences.t:
τὰ δέ κεν θεὸς ἢ τελέσειεν
ἤ κ’ ἀτέλεστ’ εἴη, ὥς οἱ φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ·
sentences.l:
and these things a god either might bring to pass
or they might be unaccomplished, as to him it has been dear in his heart;
sentences.i: and a god may either bring these things to pass or leave them unaccomplished, as it pleases him in his heart;
sentences.n: τὰ δέ is 'and these things'. κεν with the optative τελέσειεν … εἴη is a potential: 'may bring to pass … may be'. ἢ … ἤ is 'either … or', and ἀτέλεστ’ is ἀτέλεστα 'unaccomplished'. ὥς οἱ φίλον ἔπλετο θυμῷ is 'as it has been dear to him in his heart', ἔπλετο being an aorist of πέλομαι used here for what holds in general. θεός has no article, so 'a god'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come'. εἰπέ and κατάλεξον are aorist imperatives, 'tell' and 'recount'; ἀτρεκέως is 'exactly'. The line is the same as 1.169. Here the comma of the archive ends the unit, since the whole sentence would otherwise run to five lines.

sentences.t:
ὅππῃ ἀπεπλάγχθης τε καὶ ἅς τινας ἵκεο χώρας
ἀνθρώπων, αὐτούς τε πόλιάς τ’ ἐὺ ναιετοώσας,
ἠμὲν ὅσοι χαλεποί τε καὶ ἄγριοι οὐδὲ δίκαιοι,
οἵ τε φιλόξεινοι, καί σφιν νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής.
sentences.l:
where you were driven-astray, and to what lands you came
of men, both themselves and their cities well-inhabited,
both those who are harsh and savage and not just,
and those who are guest-loving, and to them a mind is god-fearing.
sentences.i: where you were driven off course, and to what lands of men you came, both the men themselves and their well-peopled cities, both those who are harsh and savage and unjust, and those who are hospitable and whose minds are god-fearing.
sentences.n: ὅππῃ is 'where'. ἀπεπλάγχθης is the aorist passive of ἀποπλάζω 'drive off course', the same verb as πλάγχθη of 1.2, with the preverb ἀπο-. ἵκεο is the aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι 'reach', second person, with the ending -εο for Attic -ου. αὐτούς … πόλιάς τ’ is 'the men themselves and their cities'; ἐὺ ναιετοώσας is 'well-inhabited'. ἠμὲν … οἵ τε is 'both … and': the second half is a relative clause, not a second ἠδέ. χαλεποί is 'harsh', ἄγριοι 'savage', δίκαιοι 'just'. φιλόξεινοι is 'guest-loving', and θεουδής 'god-fearing' (θεός and δέος 'fear'). The last two lines sort the peoples a wanderer may meet into two kinds, the second introduced by the relative οἵ τε.

sentences.t:
εἰπὲ δ’ ὅ τι κλαίεις καὶ ὀδύρεαι ἔνδοθι θυμῷ
Ἀργείων Δαναῶν ἠδ’ Ἰλίου οἶτον ἀκούων.
sentences.l:
And tell why you weep and lament within in your heart,
of the Argive Danaans and of Ilios the fate hearing.
sentences.i: And tell me why you weep and lament in your heart within, as you hear of the fate of the Argive Greeks and of Ilios.
sentences.n: ὅ τι is 'why'. ὀδύρεαι is the second person of ὀδύρομαι 'lament', uncontracted (Attic ὀδύρῃ). ἔνδοθι is 'within' (suffix -θι). ἀκούων 'hearing' has οἶτον 'fate' (the word of 489) as its object, and the genitives Ἀργείων Δαναῶν ἠδ’ Ἰλίου depend on οἶτον. Ἀργεῖοι and Δαναοί are two more names for the Greeks besides Ἀχαιοί.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ θεοὶ μὲν τεῦξαν, ἐπεκλώσαντο δ’ ὄλεθρον
ἀνθρώποις, ἵνα ᾖσι καὶ ἐσσομένοισιν ἀοιδή.
sentences.l:
That, the gods indeed made, and spun-on destruction
for men, so that there may be, for those to come, song.
sentences.i: The gods made that, and spun destruction upon men, so that there might be song for those yet to be.
sentences.n: τὸν is 'that', the fate (οἶτον) of the last unit. τεῦξαν is the aorist of τεύχω 'make', unaugmented. ἐπεκλώσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐπικλώθω 'spin upon', the image of a fate spun out by the gods. ὄλεθρον is 'destruction'. ἵνα with the subjunctive ᾖσι (from εἰμί) gives the purpose: 'so that there be song'. ἐσσομένοισιν is the dative plural of the future participle, 'for those who will be'. The gods' aim is thus said to be song, remembered by later men.

sentences.l:
Was it that some kinsman-by-marriage of yours, too, perished before Ilios,
being good, a son-in-law or a father-in-law, who especially
closest-tied are, next after blood and kin of their own?
sentences.i: Was it perhaps some relative of yours by marriage who perished before Ilios, a good man, a son-in-law or a father-in-law, who are the closest to us after a man's own blood and kin?
sentences.n: ἦ opens the question, 'was it that …?'; τοι is σοι, 'of yours'. πηός is 'a relation by marriage', which the next words spell out: γαμβρός 'son-in-law' (also brother-in-law) and πενθερός 'father-in-law'. Ἰλιόθι πρό is 'before Ilios', -θι being the suffix of place. ἀπέφθιτο is the aorist middle of ἀποφθίνω 'perish'. ἐσθλὸς ἐών is 'being good', ἐών = ὤν. οἵ τε has the epic τε of a general statement. κήδιστοι is 'closest, most nearly tied', a superlative from the family of κῆδος 'care, tie by marriage'; τελέθουσι is 'are, prove to be'; μεθ’ αἷμά τε καὶ γένος αὐτῶν is 'next after their own blood and race'. The Greek question mark ends the unit.

sentences.t:
ἦ τίς που καὶ ἑταῖρος ἀνὴρ κεχαρισμένα εἰδώς,
ἐσθλός;
sentences.l:
Or was it, perhaps, some companion man as well, knowing kindly things,
good?
sentences.i: Or was it perhaps a companion too, a man who knew kindly ways, a good one?
sentences.n: ἦ τίς που is 'or was it perhaps someone'. ἑταῖρος ἀνήρ is 'a companion, a man'. κεχαρισμένα εἰδώς, 'knowing kindly things', uses the neuter plural perfect participle of χαρίζομαι 'gratify, show favour', a phrase that pairs with πεπνυμένα εἰδῇ at 586. ἐσθλός is 'good'. The Greek question mark falls in the middle of 585, and the next unit begins with ἐπεί.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐ μέν τι κασιγνήτοιο χερείων
γίγνεται, ὅς κεν ἑταῖρος ἐὼν πεπνυμένα εἰδῇ.
sentences.l:
since not at all than a brother worse
becomes he who, as a companion, knows prudent counsels.”
sentences.i: for a companion who is versed in prudent counsels is in no way worse than a brother.”
sentences.n: ἐπεί … οὐ μέν τι is 'since surely not at all'. χερείων is the comparative 'worse', and κασιγνήτοιο (-οιο for -ου) the genitive of comparison. γίγνεται is 'proves to be'. ὅς κεν … εἰδῇ is 'whoever knows', a general relative clause with κεν and the subjunctive of οἶδα. πεπνυμένα is the neuter plural of πεπνυμένος 'prudent', with μήδεα 'counsels' understood. The closing quotation mark ends Alcinous' speech.
